L1: # `inspect` — Inspect live objects【0†¶】
L2: 
L3: Source code: 【1†Lib/inspect.py†github.com】
L4: 
L5: * * *
L6: 
L7: The `inspect` module provides several useful functions to help get information about live objects such as modules, classes, methods, functions, tracebacks, frame objects, and code objects. For example, it can help you examine the contents of a class, retrieve the source code of a method, extract and format the argument list for a function, or get all the information you need to display a detailed traceback.
L8: There are four main kinds of services provided by this module: type checking, getting source code, inspecting classes and functions, and examining the interpreter stack.
L9: ## Types and members【2†¶】
L10: 
L11: The 【3†`getmembers()`】 function retrieves the members of an object such as a class or module. The functions whose names begin with “is” are mainly provided as convenient choices for the second argument to `getmembers()`. They also help you determine when you can expect to find the following special attributes (see 【4†Import-related attributes on module objects】 for module attributes):

L18:  | __type_params__  | A tuple containing the 【5†type parameters】 of a generic class

L117: inspect.getmembers(object[, predicate])【3†¶】
L118: Return all the members of an object in a list of `(name, value)` pairs sorted by name. If the optional predicate argument—which will be called with the `value` object of each member—is supplied, only members for which the predicate returns a true value are included.
L119: 
L120: Note
L121: 
L122: `getmembers()` will only return class attributes defined in the metaclass when the argument is a class and those attributes have been listed in the metaclass’ custom 【9†`__dir__()`】.
L123: inspect.getmembers_static(object[, predicate])【10†¶】
L124: 
L125: 
L126: Return all the members of an object in a list of `(name, value)` pairs sorted by name without triggering dynamic lookup via the descriptor protocol, __getattr__ or __getattribute__. Optionally, only return members that satisfy a given predicate.
L127: 
L128: Note
L129: `getmembers_static()` may not be able to retrieve all members that getmembers can fetch (like dynamically created attributes) and may find members that getmembers can’t (like descriptors that raise AttributeError). It can also return descriptor objects instead of instance members in some cases.
L130: 
L131: Added in version 3.11.
L132: 
L133: inspect.getmodulename(path)【11†¶】
L134: Return the name of the module named by the file path, without including the names of enclosing packages. The file extension is checked against all of the entries in 【12†`importlib.machinery.all_suffixes()`】. If it matches, the final path component is returned with the extension removed. Otherwise, `None` is returned.
L135: 
L136: Note that this function only returns a meaningful name for actual Python modules - paths that potentially refer to Python packages will still return `None`.
L137: Changed in version 3.3: The function is based directly on 【13†`importlib`】.
L138: 
L139: inspect.ismodule(object)【14†¶】
L140: 
L141: 
L142: Return `True` if the object is a module.
L143: 
L144: inspect.isclass(object)【15†¶】
L145: 
L146: 
L147: Return `True` if the object is a class, whether built-in or created in Python code.
L148: 
L149: This function returns `False` for 【16†generic aliases】 of classes, such as `list[int]`.
L150: 
L151: inspect.ismethod(object)【17†¶】
L152: 
L153: 
L154: Return `True` if the object is a bound method written in Python.
L155: 
L156: Note
L157: For example, given this class:
L158: 
L159:     >>> class Greeter:
L160:     ...     def say_hello(self):
L161:     ...         print('hello!')
L162: A bound method (also known as an instance method) is created when accessing `say_hello` (a 【18†function】 defined in the `Greeter` namespace) through an instance of the `Greeter` class:
L163: 
L164:     >>> instance = Greeter()
L165: 
L166:     >>> instance.say_hello
L167:     <bound method Greeter.say_hello of <__main__.Greeter object ...>>
L168:     >>> ismethod(instance.say_hello)
L169:     True
L170:     >>> isfunction(instance.say_hello)
L171:     False
L172: Accessing `say_hello` through the `Greeter` class will return the function itself. For this function, `ismethod()` will return `False`, but 【19†`isfunction()`】 will return `True`:
L173: 
L174:     >>> Greeter.say_hello
L175:     <function Greeter.say_hello at 0x7f7503854a90>
L176:     >>> ismethod(Greeter.say_hello)
L177:     False
L178:     >>> isfunction(Greeter.say_hello)
L179:     True
L180: 
L181: 
L182: See 【20†Methods】 for details.
L183: 
L184: inspect.isfunction(object)【19†¶】
L185: Return `True` if the object is a Python function, which includes functions created by a 【21†lambda】 expression.
L186: 
L187: See the note for 【17†`ismethod()`】 for an example.
L188: 
L189: inspect.ispackage(object)【22†¶】
L190: 
L191: 
L192: Return `True` if the object is a 【23†package】.
L193: 
L194: Added in version 3.14.
L195: 
L196: inspect.isgeneratorfunction(object)【24†¶】
L197: 
L198: 
L199: Return `True` if the object is a Python generator function.
L200: 
L201: It also returns `True` for bound methods created from Python generator functions (see 【20†Methods】 for more information).
L202: Changed in version 3.8: Functions wrapped in 【25†`functools.partial()`】 now return `True` if the wrapped function is a Python generator function.
L203: 
L204: Changed in version 3.10.6: 【26†Duck-typed】 function-like objects now return `True` if their code object has the 【27†`CO_GENERATOR`】 flag.
L205: 
L206: Changed in version 3.13: Functions wrapped in 【28†`functools.partialmethod()`】 now return `True` if the wrapped function is a Python generator function.
L207: 
L208: inspect.isgenerator(object)【29†¶】
L209: Return `True` if the object is a generator.
L210: 
L211: inspect.iscoroutinefunction(object)【30†¶】
L212: 
L213: 
L214: Return `True` if the object is a 【31†coroutine function】 (a function defined with an 【32†`async def`】 syntax), a 【25†`functools.partial()`】 wrapping a coroutine function, or a sync function marked with 【33†`markcoroutinefunction()`】.
L215: 
L216: Added in version 3.5.
L217: 
L218: Changed in version 3.8: Functions wrapped in 【25†`functools.partial()`】 now return `True` if the wrapped function is a 【31†coroutine function】.
L219: Changed in version 3.10.6: 【26†Duck-typed】 function-like objects now return `True` if their code object has the 【34†`CO_COROUTINE`】 flag.
L220: 
L221: Changed in version 3.12: Sync functions marked with 【33†`markcoroutinefunction()`】 now return `True`.
L222: 
L223: Changed in version 3.13: Functions wrapped in 【28†`functools.partialmethod()`】 now return `True` if the wrapped function is a 【31†coroutine function】.
L224: 
L225: inspect.markcoroutinefunction(func)【33†¶】
L226: Decorator to mark a callable as a 【31†coroutine function】 if it would not otherwise be detected by 【30†`iscoroutinefunction()`】.
L227: 
L228: This may be of use for sync functions that return a 【35†coroutine】, if the function is passed to an API that requires 【30†`iscoroutinefunction()`】.
L229: 
L230: When possible, using an 【32†`async def`】 function is preferred. Also acceptable is calling the function and testing the return with 【36†`iscoroutine()`】.
L231: 
L232: Added in version 3.12.
L233: 
L234: inspect.iscoroutine(object)【36†¶】
L235: Return `True` if the object is a 【35†coroutine】 created by an 【32†`async def`】 function.
L236: 
L237: Added in version 3.5.
L238: 
L239: inspect.isawaitable(object)【37†¶】
L240: 
L241: 
L242: Return `True` if the object can be used in 【38†`await`】 expression.
L243: 
L244: Can also be used to distinguish generator-based coroutines from regular generators:
L245: 
L246:     import types
L247: 
L248:     def gen():
L249:         yield
L250:     @types.coroutine
L251:     def gen_coro():
L252:         yield
L253: 
L254:     assert not isawaitable(gen())
L255:     assert isawaitable(gen_coro())
L256: Added in version 3.5.
L257: 
L258: inspect.isasyncgenfunction(object)【39†¶】
L259: 
L260: 
L261: Return `True` if the object is an 【40†asynchronous generator】 function, for example:
L262: 
L263:     >>> async def agen():
L264:     ...     yield 1
L265:     ...
L266:     >>> inspect.isasyncgenfunction(agen)
L267:     True
L268: 
L269: 
L270: Added in version 3.6.
L271: 
L272: Changed in version 3.8: Functions wrapped in 【25†`functools.partial()`】 now return `True` if the wrapped function is an 【40†asynchronous generator】 function.
L273: Changed in version 3.10.6: 【26†Duck-typed】 function-like objects now return `True` if their code object has the 【41†`CO_ASYNC_GENERATOR`】 flag.
L274: 
L275: Changed in version 3.13: Functions wrapped in 【28†`functools.partialmethod()`】 now return `True` if the wrapped function is a 【40†asynchronous generator】 function.
L276: 
L277: inspect.isasyncgen(object)【42†¶】
L278: 
L279: 
L280: Return `True` if the object is an 【43†asynchronous generator iterator】 created by an 【40†asynchronous generator】 function.
L281: 
L282: Added in version 3.6.
L283: inspect.istraceback(object)【44†¶】
L284: 
L285: 
L286: Return `True` if the object is a traceback.
L287: 
L288: inspect.isframe(object)【45†¶】
L289: 
L290: 
L291: Return `True` if the object is a frame.
L292: 
L293: inspect.iscode(object)【46†¶】
L294: 
L295: 
L296: Return `True` if the object is a code.
L297: 
L298: inspect.isbuiltin(object)【47†¶】
L299: 
L300: 
L301: Return `True` if the object is a built-in function or a bound built-in method.
L302: 
L303: inspect.ismethodwrapper(object)【48†¶】
L304: 
L305: 
L306: Return `True` if the type of object is a 【49†`MethodWrapperType`】.
L307: These are instances of 【49†`MethodWrapperType`】, such as 【50†`__str__()`】, 【51†`__eq__()`】 and 【52†`__repr__()`】.
L308: 
L309: Added in version 3.11.
L310: 
L311: inspect.isroutine(object)【53†¶】
L312: 
L313: 
L314: Return `True` if the object is a user-defined or built-in function or method.
L315: 
L316: inspect.isabstract(object)【54†¶】
L317: 
L318: 
L319: Return `True` if the object is an abstract base class.
L320: 
L321: inspect.ismethoddescriptor(object)【55†¶】
L322: Return `True` if the object is a method descriptor, but not if 【15†`isclass()`】, 【17†`ismethod()`】 or 【19†`isfunction()`】 is true.
L323: 
L324: This, for example, is true of `int.__add__`. An object passing this test has a 【56†`__get__()`】 method, but not a 【57†`__set__()`】 method or a 【58†`__delete__()`】 method. Beyond that, the set of attributes varies. A 【59†`__name__`】 attribute is usually sensible, and 【60†`__doc__`】 often is.
L325: Method descriptors that also pass any of the other tests (`isclass()`, `ismethod()` or `isfunction()`) make this function return `False`, simply because those other tests promise more – you can, for example, count on having the 【61†`__func__`】 attribute when an object passes 【17†`ismethod()`】.
L326: Changed in version 3.13: This function no longer incorrectly reports objects with 【56†`__get__()`】 and 【58†`__delete__()`】, but not 【57†`__set__()`】, as being method descriptors (such objects are data descriptors, not method descriptors).
L327: 
L328: inspect.isdatadescriptor(object)【62†¶】
L329: 
L330: 
L331: Return `True` if the object is a data descriptor, but not if 【15†`isclass()`】, 【17†`ismethod()`】 or 【19†`isfunction()`】 is true.
L332: Data descriptors always have a 【57†`__set__()`】 method and/or a 【58†`__delete__()`】 method. Optionally, they may also have a 【56†`__get__()`】 method.
L333: 
L334: Examples of data descriptors are 【63†`properties`】, getsets and member descriptors. Note that for the latter two (defined only in C extension modules), more specific tests are available: 【64†`isgetsetdescriptor()`】 and 【65†`ismemberdescriptor()`】, respectively.
L335: While data descriptors may also have 【59†`__name__`】 and `__doc__` attributes (as properties, getsets and member descriptors do), this is not necessarily the case in general.
L336: Changed in version 3.8: This function now reports objects with only a 【57†`__set__()`】 method as being data descriptors (the presence of 【56†`__get__()`】 is no longer required for that). Moreover, objects with 【58†`__delete__()`】, but not `__set__()`, are now properly recognized as data descriptors as well, which was not the case previously.
L337: 
L338: inspect.isgetsetdescriptor(object)【64†¶】
L339: 
L340: 
L341: Return `True` if the object is a getset descriptor.
L342: CPython implementation detail: getsets are attributes defined in extension modules via 【66†`PyGetSetDef`】 structures. For Python implementations without such types, this method will always return `False`.
L343: 
L344: inspect.ismemberdescriptor(object)【65†¶】
L345: 
L346: 
L347: Return `True` if the object is a member descriptor.
L348: CPython implementation detail: Member descriptors are attributes defined in extension modules via 【67†`PyMemberDef`】 structures. For Python implementations without such types, this method will always return `False`.
L349: ## Retrieving source code【68†¶】
L350: 
L351: inspect.getdoc(object, * (Keyword-only parameters separator (PEP 3102)), inherit_class_doc=True, fallback_to_class_doc=True)【69†¶】
L352: 
L353: 
L354: Get the documentation string for an object, cleaned up with 【70†`cleandoc()`】. If the documentation string for an object is not provided:
L355: 
L356:   * if the object is a class and inherit_class_doc is true (by default), retrieve the documentation string from the inheritance hierarchy;
L357:   * if the object is a method, a property or a descriptor, retrieve the documentation string from the inheritance hierarchy;
L358: 
L359:   * otherwise, if fallback_to_class_doc is true (by default), retrieve the documentation string from the class of the object.
L360: 
L361: Return `None` if the documentation string is invalid or missing.
L362: 
L363: Changed in version 3.5: Documentation strings are now inherited if not overridden.
L364: 
L365: Changed in version 3.15: Added parameters inherit_class_doc and fallback_to_class_doc.
L366: Documentation strings on 【71†`cached_property`】 objects are now inherited if not overridden.
L367: 
L368: inspect.getcomments(object)【72†¶】
L369: 
L370: 
L371: Return in a single string any lines of comments immediately preceding the object’s source code (for a class, function, or method), or at the top of the Python source file (if the object is a module). If the object’s source code is unavailable, return `None`. This could happen if the object has been defined in C or the interactive shell.
L372: 
L373: inspect.getfile(object)【73†¶】
L374: Return the name of the (text or binary) file in which an object was defined. An 【74†`OSError`】 is raised if the source code cannot be retrieved. This will fail with a 【75†`TypeError`】 if the object is a built-in module, class, or function.
L375: 
L376: inspect.getmodule(object)【76†¶】
L377: 
L378: 
L379: Try to guess which module an object was defined in. Return `None` if the module cannot be determined.
L380: 
L381: inspect.getsourcefile(object)【77†¶】
L382: Return the name of the Python source file in which an object was defined or `None` if no way can be identified to get the source. An 【74†`OSError`】 is raised if the source code cannot be retrieved. This will fail with a 【75†`TypeError`】 if the object is a built-in module, class, or function.
L383: 
L384: inspect.getsourcelines(object)【78†¶】
L385: Return a list of source lines and starting line number for an object. The argument may be a module, class, method, function, traceback, frame, or code object. The source code is returned as a list of the lines corresponding to the object and the line number indicates where in the original source file the first line of code was found. An 【74†`OSError`】 is raised if the source code cannot be retrieved. A 【75†`TypeError`】 is raised if the object is a built-in module, class, or function.
L386: Changed in version 3.3: 【74†`OSError`】 is raised instead of 【79†`IOError`】, now an alias of the former.
L387: 
L388: inspect.getsource(object)【80†¶】
L389: 
L390: 
L391: Return the text of the source code for an object. The argument may be a module, class, method, function, traceback, frame, or code object. The source code is returned as a single string. An 【74†`OSError`】 is raised if the source code cannot be retrieved. A 【75†`TypeError`】 is raised if the object is a built-in module, class, or function.
L392: Changed in version 3.3: 【74†`OSError`】 is raised instead of 【79†`IOError`】, now an alias of the former.
L393: 
L394: inspect.cleandoc(doc)【70†¶】
L395: 
L396: 
L397: Clean up indentation from docstrings that are indented to line up with blocks of code.
L398: 
L399: All leading whitespace is removed from the first line. Any leading whitespace that can be uniformly removed from the second line onwards is removed. Empty lines at the beginning and end are subsequently removed. Also, all tabs are expanded to spaces.
L400: ## Introspecting callables with the Signature object【81†¶】
L401: 
L402: Added in version 3.3.
L403: 
L404: The 【82†`Signature`】 object represents the call signature of a callable object and its return annotation. To retrieve a `Signature` object, use the `signature()` function.

L406: inspect.signature(callable, * (Keyword-only parameters separator (PEP 3102)), follow_wrapped=True, globals=None, locals=None, eval_str=False, annotation_format=Format.VALUE)【83†¶】
L407: Return a 【82†`Signature`】 object for the given callable:
L408: 
L409:     >>> from inspect import signature
L410:     >>> def foo(a, *, b:int, **kwargs):
L411:     ...     pass
L412: 
L413:     >>> sig = signature(foo)
L414: 
L415:     >>> str(sig)
L416:     '(a, *, b: int, **kwargs)'
L417: 
L418:     >>> str(sig.parameters['b'])
L419:     'b: int'
L420: 
L421:     >>> sig.parameters['b'].annotation
L422:     <class 'int'>
L423:

L425: Accepts a wide range of Python callables, from plain functions and classes to 【25†`functools.partial()`】 objects.
L426: If some of the annotations are strings (e.g., because `from __future__ import annotations` was used), `signature()` will attempt to automatically un-stringize the annotations using 【84†`annotationlib.get_annotations()`】. The globals, locals, and eval_str parameters are passed into `annotationlib.get_annotations()` when resolving the annotations; see the documentation for `annotationlib.get_annotations()` for instructions on how to use these parameters.
L427: A member of the 【85†`annotationlib.Format`】 enum can be passed to the annotation_format parameter to control the format of the returned annotations. For example, use `annotation_format=annotationlib.Format.STRING` to return annotations in string format.
L428: Raises 【86†`ValueError`】 if no signature can be provided, and 【75†`TypeError`】 if that type of object is not supported. Also, if the annotations are stringized, and eval_str is not false, the `eval()` call(s) to un-stringize the annotations in 【84†`annotationlib.get_annotations()`】 could potentially raise any kind of exception.

L443: 
L444: A `Signature` object represents the call signature of a function and its return annotation. For each parameter accepted by the function it stores a 【88†`Parameter`】 object in its 【89†`parameters`】 collection.
L445: The optional parameters argument is a sequence of 【88†`Parameter`】 objects, which is validated to check that there are no parameters with duplicate names, and that the parameters are in the right order, i.e. positional-only first, then positional-or-keyword, and that parameters with defaults follow parameters without defaults.
L446: 
L447: The optional return_annotation argument can be an arbitrary Python object. It represents the “return” annotation of the callable.
L448: `Signature` objects are immutable. Use 【90†`Signature.replace()`】 or 【91†`copy.replace()`】 to make a modified copy.
L449: 
L450: Changed in version 3.5: `Signature` objects are now picklable and 【92†hashable】.

L457: parameters【89†¶】

L460: An ordered mapping of parameters’ names to the corresponding 【88†`Parameter`】 objects. Parameters appear in strict definition order, including keyword-only parameters.
L461: Changed in version 3.7: Python only explicitly guaranteed that it preserved the declaration order of keyword-only parameters as of version 3.7, although in practice this order had always been preserved in Python 3.

L466: The “return” annotation for the callable. If the callable has no “return” annotation, this attribute is set to 【93†`Signature.empty`】.
